sections.title: Story
sections.narration: You avoid uncomfortable questions in daily life. Ancient Greeks believed examining questions was essential for the soul. In the 1960s, psychologist Lawrence Kohlberg studied about 300 children and measured moral stages. So why do we ignore Socrates' call to examine ourselves? He argued the unexamined life is not worth living. The result? Modern studies link self‑questioning to higher moral development. In 2015, Jonathan Haidt and NYU researchers surveyed about 1,200 adults. They found roughly 80% made moral judgments intuitively first. Later reflection only adjusted those initial choices modestly. Does that mean questioning is useless? No, because questioning builds deeper understanding. In 2014, Michigan psychologists found reflective dialogue boosted abstract reasoning by about 12 points. That's it. Research also shows that daily self‑questioning raises life satisfaction by about 20%. Your brain will thank you with clearer decisions and calmer emotions. So next time you dodge a tough question, remember Socrates’ test. You avoid uncomfortable questions in daily life.
